newsitem.title: JAPAN: Beatles memorabilia sale flops in Japan.
newsitem.headline: Beatles memorabilia sale flops in Japan.

text.p: The original birth certificate of Sir Paul McCartney sold for 10.35 million yen ($84,146) but it was a hard day's night after that on Saturday in the biggest-ever auction of Beatles memorabilia.

In a sale marked by controversy and failure to meet hopes of world record prices, bidders in Tokyo and London snapped up small mementos of the Fab Four but signalled the Liverpool Lads' comeback in pop charts did not extend to the auction circuit.
The memorabilia came from relatives of the Beatles, people who worked with them and collectors eager to cash in on a new wave of Beatle popularity from their "Anthology" series.

McCartney's certificate, the first of 300 items to go on the block in a five-hour sale, brought a far higher price than the pre-sale estimate of $13,000. The sale price includes the 15 percent commission for the auction house.
The unidentified buyer was in London while the seller was a record collector from California, auction house officials said.

Speculation was rife in the Tokyo audience that McCartney, who has singled out his lack of ownership of his birth certificate as an example of an unsavoury trade in pop music memorabilia, might have used an agent in London to buy back the document.

"To show how ridiculous this whole meomorabilia market has become, there is currently someone in the United States who owns my own birth certificate," McCartney said recently. "How people can feel that that is right is beyond my comprehension."
The certificate, which records McCartney's June 18, 1942, birth in Liverpool, England, had first been sold by McCartney's stepmother after the death of his father.
Even if McCartney does not turn out to be the buyer of the certificate, he was successful in stopping part of the sale.
On Friday he obtained an injunction against Bonhams, which organised the auction, to halt the planned sale of the original lyrics to "Penny Lane," one of the Beatles' biggest hits.
Geoff Baker, spokesman for the recently knighted Beatle, said he believed the owner of the Number One hit was not entitled to sell the draft, which had been valued at $79,780.
In another setback, a Ringo Starr drum skin was withdrawn after questions were raised about its authenticity.
Three decades after Beatlemania swept Japan and the rest of the world, Tokyo was chosen as the site of Saturday's auction because the music is again topping charts in Japan.

But in a statement probably as much about the end of the good economic times in Japan as the popularity of Beatles mementos, the two items expected to fetch the highest prices failed to meet their reserve prices.

They were John Lennon's 1970 Mercedes Benz limousine, which attracted a top bid of only 40 million yen ($330,000) when there were forecasts of a $1 million sale and a Steinway piano on which Lennon composed his hit song "Imagine."
Bids for the piano, expected to fetch up to $500,000, barely reached half that figure.
Another top item, the piano on which Lennon composed "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds", was withdrawn from the auction at the last minute when the seller suddenly doubled the reserve price.
However there were some successes.
The small Liverpool home where Ringo Starr was born went for $22,000, several thousand dollars more than expected.

Ted Owen, pop and rock expert for Bonhams, said the high prices paid for smaller items, from a 2.76 sterling check signed by George Harrison to a used Lennon guitar strap, made up for disappointment at the absence of sales of the major items.
"The Beatles are still Number one in rock memorabilia," he said. "Perhaps some sellers had too high expectations."
